questions.stem: Alan Turing's 1950 operational test for intelligent behaviour is commonly known as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Turing's Imitation Game / Turing Test

questions.stem: Which four capability areas are listed as prerequisites for a machine to pass the Turing Test?

choices.A: Computer vision, robotics, databases, and cryptography
choices.B: Search, CSP, hill climbing, and linear regression
choices.C: Sensors, actuators, architecture, and program only
choices.D: NLP, knowledge representation, automated reasoning, and machine learning

questions.explanation: NLP, KR, automated reasoning, ML listed as prerequisites

questions.stem: In the four dimensions of AI, "acting rationally" emphasises which idea?

choices.A: Matching human cognitive errors and biases
choices.B: Achieving the optimal expected outcome given available information
choices.C: Simulating the physical brain with imaging data
choices.D: Passing as human in conversation only

questions.explanation: Rational ideal = right/optimal expected outcome

questions.stem: Cognitive science (thinking humanly) is described as which kind of approach?

choices.A: Top-down using computer models and experimental psychology

questions.explanation: Deep Blue framed as search algorithms win

questions.stem: AlphaGo defeating Lee Sedol (2016) is attributed in the slides primarily to demonstrating the power of what?
questions.explanation: AlphaGo linked to deep RL

questions.stem: Which comparison is correct for Symbolic AI (GOFAI)?

choices.A: Pros: black-box accuracy; Cons: needs no training data

choices.D: Often opaque ("black box") and need large labelled datasets

choices.B: Whether the Turing Test is passed

questions.explanation: Frontier (Sibiu, Timisoara, Zerind)

questions.stem: Breadth-first search (BFS) expands which nodes and implements the frontier how?

choices.B: Least g-cost nodes; priority queue by g

questions.stem: BFS completeness and optimality (as stated for equal step costs) are:

choices.B: Complete only in infinite spaces; optimal always for uneven costs
choices.C: Complete for DFS only; optimal for greedy search
choices.D: Complete if b and d finite; optimal if step costs are all equal

questions.stem: BFS time and space complexity (standard slide summary) are both:
questions.explanation: Time and space O(bd)

choices.B: It cannot use a FIFO frontier
choices.D: Space is the bigger problem (than time)

questions.explanation: Space bigger problem than time

questions.stem: BFS finds the shortest path in terms of number of transitions. Relative to least cost paths when costs differ, BFS:

choices.A: Always finds the least cost path
choices.B: Is identical to A* with any heuristic
choices.C: Is identical to DFS with loops
choices.D: Does not find the least cost path in general

questions.explanation: BFS not least-cost when costs differ

questions.stem: Uniform-Cost Search (UCS) differs from BFS mainly because:

choices.C: It expands by lowest h(n) only
choices.D: Frontier is a priority queue ordered by path cost g; goal test when selected for expansion

questions.explanation: Priority by g; goal test on expand

questions.stem: UCS completeness and optimality conditions stated include:

choices.B: Complete only if h is admissible
choices.C: Complete if each step has minimal cost >= epsilon; optimal yes

questions.explanation: Complete if step cost >= epsilon; optimal

questions.stem: Depth-first search (DFS) implements the frontier as:

choices.C: Priority queue by f = g + h

questions.explanation: LIFO stack

questions.stem: DFS properties as summarised: complete? optimal? space?

choices.B: No (fails in infinite-depth/loops); No; O(bm) linear space
choices.C: Yes always; Yes; exponential space only
choices.D: Complete like BFS; Optimal like UCS; O(1) space

questions.explanation: Incomplete in general; not optimal; O(bm) space

questions.stem: Depth-limited search is:

choices.B: DFS with depth limit l (nodes at depth l have no successors)

questions.explanation: DFS with depth limit l

questions.stem: Iterative-deepening search (IDS) works by:

choices.A: Keeping increasing the depth limit l until a solution is found

questions.explanation: Increase l until solution found

questions.stem: Practical guidance from the uninformed search summary includes:

choices.A: Prefer DFS when solutions are short; prefer BFS when many solutions
choices.B: Always prefer plain DFS in infinite spaces without checks
choices.C: Prefer BFS when solutions are short; prefer DFS when many solutions exist; IDS uses linear space

questions.explanation: BFS for short solutions; DFS if many; IDS linear space

questions.explanation: UCS returns lowest-cost path

choices.C: Estimate how far a state is from a goal (or cost to reach the goal)

questions.explanation: Expand lowest f estimate

choices.A: Straight-line distance from n to Bucharest
choices.B: Sum of step costs so far

choices.A: Not complete in general (can loop); not optimal
choices.C: Same guarantees as A* with any h

questions.stem: A* search evaluation function is:
questions.explanation: f = g + h

choices.A: Estimated cost to goal; cost so far
choices.B: Cost so far to reach n; estimated cost to goal from n

questions.stem: Iterative deepening runs depth-limited search with limit 0, then 1, then 2, and so on, until a goal is found. Which statement is correct?

questions.stem: A heuristic h never exceeds the true remaining cost to a goal. On at least one edge, h(n) > cost(n, n') + h(n'). A* may be run as tree search, or as graph search that drops repeated states. Which conclusion follows?

choices.B: h is inadmissible, so neither version is optimal
choices.C: h is consistent but not admissible, so only graph search is optimal
choices.D: h is admissible but not consistent. Tree-search A* is optimal. Graph-search A* is not guaranteed to be optimal

questions.explanation: h <= true cost is admissibility, which is enough for optimal tree search. The broken triangle inequality means h is not consistent, so graph search can close a state before the cheaper path arrives.

questions.stem: h1 and h2 are both admissible, and h2(n) >= h1(n) for every node, with h2 not identical to h1. For A* on the same problem, which claim holds?

choices.B: h2 is inadmissible, because a larger heuristic must overestimate somewhere
choices.C: A* with h1 expands fewer nodes, because a smaller heuristic is more accurate
choices.D: h2 is inconsistent, because dominance breaks the triangle inequality

questions.explanation: A larger admissible heuristic is closer to the true cost without crossing it, so it expands no more nodes except possibly on the f = C* contour.

questions.stem: For the 8-puzzle, consider the relaxation that keeps "move to an adjacent square" and drops "the destination must be blank". The exact cost of that relaxed puzzle is used as h. Which heuristic is that, and why is it admissible?

choices.C: The path cost g. It is admissible because g is exact
choices.D: The true remaining solution length. A* then expands only the goal

questions.stem: Backtracking is choosing the next variable. X and Y each have 2 legal values left. X shares constraints with 3 other unassigned variables. Y shares a constraint with 1 other unassigned variable. Which choice matches the course heuristics?

questions.stem: Labels are 0 and 1. Predict 1 when w · x >= 0, otherwise 0. Update only when the prediction is wrong: w <- w + alpha * (y - y_hat) * x. Now w = [1, -1, 0], x = [2, 1, 1], y = 0, and alpha = 0.5. The third component is the bias, and the third feature is 1. What is w after this example?
questions.explanation: The dot product is 2 - 1 + 0 = 1, so the prediction is 1 and the label 0 is a mistake. Add 0.5 * (0 - 1) * [2, 1, 1], which subtracts [1, 0.5, 0.5] and leaves [0, -1.5, -0.5].

questions.stem: A feed-forward net computes h = W1 x + b1 and then y = W2 h + b2. There is no non-linearity between the two layers. Which conclusion follows?

Attribute A splits the rows into two children of equal size, and each child has entropy 0.811. Attribute B splits the rows into two children of equal size, and each child has entropy 0. Which attribute should ID3 pick at this node?
questions.explanation: Gain(A) = 1 - 0.811 = 0.189. Gain(B) = 1 - 0 = 1. The pure split wins. Gain 0 would mean the children were as mixed as the parent.

questions.stem: A Bayes-net node is binary and has three binary parents. Its conditional probability table has one distribution for each parent assignment, and each of those distributions sums to 1. How many free parameters does the table have?
questions.explanation: Eight parent assignments, and a binary row has 2 - 1 = 1 free number, so 8. Sixteen counts both entries in every row. The row sum removes one of them.

questions.stem: A Bayes net's joint probability is the product of one local conditional per node. For one assignment the factors are P(B) = 0.001, P(not E) = 0.998, P(A | B, not E) = 0.94, P(not J | A) = 0.1, and P(not M | A) = 0.3. What is that joint probability, rounded to six decimal places?

The Q-learning update is Q(s, a) <- (1 - alpha) * Q(s, a) + alpha * [r + gamma * max over a' of Q(s', a')]. Use alpha = 0.5 and gamma = 0.9. Before the update, Q(s, a) = 2. The sample is r = 1 and next state s'. Q(s', left) = 4 and Q(s', right) = 1. The behaviour policy took right in s'. What is Q(s, a) after the update?
questions.explanation: The max in s' is 4, even though the behaviour policy took right. Target = 1 + 0.9 * 4 = 4.6. New Q = 0.5 * 2 + 0.5 * 4.6 = 3.3. Using right instead of the max gives 1.95.

questions.stem: The discount factor is gamma = 0.5. From now on, every step returns reward +1, and the process never ends. The return is the sum from t = 0 to infinity of (gamma^t) * 1. What is that return?
questions.explanation: The infinite geometric sum 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + ... equals 1 / (1 - 0.5) = 2. Gamma must be below 1 for that sum to be finite.

questions.stem: The VC dimension of a classifier family is the size of the largest set of points that family can shatter: for every way of labelling those points, some classifier in the family labels them perfectly. In this course a perceptron in the plane has VC dimension 3. Which reading matches that definition?

choices.A: Any training set of 3 points is memorised, so the test error on those points is zero, and this is how you choose a learning rate
choices.B: The gap between training error and test error is 3 percent
choices.C: XOR is linearly separable, because a VC dimension of 3 is only a bound on training time

questions.explanation: Shattering three points in general position, and failing on an XOR labelling of four points, is the VC-dimension-3 fact for a planar perceptron. It is not a recipe for setting the learning rate.

questions.stem: Mean squared error on n examples is (1/n) times the sum of squared residuals.
questions.explanation: MSE averages the squared residuals.

questions.stem: The gradient of a loss points in the direction of steepest decrease.
questions.explanation: The gradient points toward steepest increase, so descent subtracts it.

questions.stem: With the bias folded into w, the linear-regression closed form is w* = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y.
questions.explanation: That normal equation is the closed form once bias is absorbed into w.

questions.stem: A learning rate that is too large only slows gradient descent. It does not cause divergence.
questions.explanation: Too large an eta causes divergence or oscillation. Too small an eta is the slow case.

questions.stem: The perceptron step function is not trained by ordinary gradient descent, because its gradient is 0 almost everywhere.
questions.explanation: The step is flat except at 0, where the derivative is undefined.

questions.stem: Passing a linear score through a sigmoid makes the logistic-regression decision boundary non-linear.
questions.explanation: The sigmoid gives a probability. The decision boundary of logistic regression is still linear.

questions.stem: Softmax regression predicts the class with the largest score.
questions.explanation: The predicted class is argmax of the class scores.

questions.stem: Full gradient descent updates from a mini-batch of 32 to 512 examples.
questions.explanation: Full gradient descent uses every training example. Mini-batches belong to stochastic gradient descent.

questions.stem: If the training set is not linearly separable, perceptron weights need not converge.
questions.explanation: The convergence theorem needs linear separability.

questions.stem: The lecture treats squared error as the loss for multi-class classification.
questions.explanation: Squared error is the regression loss. Multi-class classification uses cross-entropy.

questions.stem: Without a non-linear activation, a stack of linear layers collapses to one linear map.
questions.explanation: Non-linearity is what stops the stack collapsing to one linear map.

questions.stem: XOR becomes linearly separable once a single perceptron is given a bias term.
questions.explanation: XOR is not linearly separable. A bias does not fix a single perceptron.

questions.stem: For a sigmoid output y, the factor y(1-y) is largest at y = 0.5, where it equals 0.25.
questions.explanation: The sigmoid derivative s(1-s) peaks at 0.25 when s = 0.5.

questions.stem: The momentum term on the slide uses the next weight, w(t+1) - w(t+2).
questions.explanation: Momentum adds eta * (w(t) - w(t-1)), the previous step.

questions.stem: Back-propagation is gradient descent together with the chain rule.
questions.explanation: Errors are sent backward with the chain rule, and weights step by gradient descent.

questions.stem: The voice-recognition sketch uses 6 inputs, 60 hidden units, and 2 outputs.
questions.explanation: The sketch is 60 inputs, 6 hidden units, and 2 outputs.

questions.stem: The lecture initialises weights to random numbers in [-1, 1].
questions.explanation: The stated initialisation range is [-1, 1].

questions.stem: The output-unit delta is y(1-y)(y - z), where y is the target and z is the sigmoid output.
questions.explanation: For an output unit, delta = y(1-y)(z-y), where y is the sigmoid output and z is the target.

questions.stem: The factor 1/2 in the squared-error loss makes the derivative equal to (prediction - target) rather than twice that.
questions.explanation: The 1/2 cancels the 2 from differentiating a square.

questions.stem: Each neuron in these feed-forward nets connects to only one neuron in the next layer.
questions.explanation: The feed-forward nets in the lecture are fully connected.

questions.stem: Validation error is for choosing hyperparameters. The test set should be used once.
questions.explanation: Do not tune on the test set.

questions.stem: Overfitting means training error and test error are both high because the model is too simple.
questions.explanation: That pattern is underfitting. Overfitting is low training error and high test error.

questions.stem: A perceptron in two dimensions has VC dimension 3.
questions.explanation: It can shatter 3 points and cannot realise XOR on 4 points.

questions.stem: Early stopping keeps the weights from the last epoch, because that is when training loss is lowest.
questions.explanation: Keep the weights from the best validation epoch. Patience then restores those weights.

questions.stem: Soft weight decay adds (lambda/2) times the squared weight norm to the loss.
questions.explanation: The soft penalty is (lambda/2) * ||w||^2.

questions.stem: As lambda goes to infinity, the optimal weights grow without bound.
questions.explanation: As lambda goes to infinity, the optimal weights go to 0.

questions.stem: Typical dropout rates on the slides are about 0.2 to 0.5 on hidden layers.
questions.explanation: Hidden-layer dropout on the slides is about 0.2 to 0.5. Input dropout is about 0.1.

questions.stem: A residual connection is one of the four regularisation methods in this lecture.
questions.explanation: Residual connections help optimisation. They are not one of the four regularisers.

questions.stem: In K-fold cross-validation, each fold is trained on the other K-1 parts, and the K validation errors are averaged.
questions.explanation: Typical K is 5 or 10, and the reported figure is the average validation error.

questions.stem: In the blue-shirt loan story, a spurious feature cannot make training error look good.
questions.explanation: Training error can look excellent while the shirt-colour rule fails on new applicants.

questions.stem: ID3 splits on the attribute with the largest information gain.
questions.explanation: IMPORTANCE in this lecture is maximum information gain.

questions.stem: A pure set of labels has entropy 1 bit.
questions.explanation: A pure set has entropy 0. An even Boolean split has entropy 1.

questions.stem: Information gain is the parent entropy minus the weighted average of the child entropies.
questions.explanation: Gain is I(parent) minus the size-weighted child entropies.

questions.stem: ID3 returns a tree that is guaranteed to be the smallest possible tree.
questions.explanation: The search is greedy. The result is a small consistent tree, not a proven smallest tree.

questions.stem: Gain ratio divides information gain by a term that penalises attributes with many values.
questions.explanation: The extra division penalises attributes such as a unique identifier.

questions.stem: If no attributes remain and the remaining examples are mixed, ID3 returns the positive class.
questions.explanation: Mixed examples with no attributes left return the majority class.

questions.stem: In the restaurant example, Patrons is chosen as the root because it has the highest gain.
questions.explanation: With p = n = 6, parent entropy is 1, and Patrons has the highest gain.

questions.stem: A fair coin has entropy 0.
questions.explanation: A fair coin has entropy 1 bit. A coin that always lands heads has entropy 0.

questions.stem: Refusing a split whose information gain is below a threshold is one way to limit overfitting.
questions.explanation: A gain threshold, and pruning, both limit splits that only fit the training sample.

questions.stem: Continuous numeric outputs are the ordinary target for the classification trees in this lecture.
questions.explanation: Continuous outputs take the method outside ordinary classification trees.

questions.stem: Each probability is at least 0, and the probabilities in one distribution sum to 1.
questions.explanation: Non-negativity and summing to 1 are required of a distribution.

questions.stem: A joint table over n variables, each with domain size d, has n times d entries.
questions.explanation: The joint table has d^n entries, which is why it is impractical.

questions.stem: The definition P(a|b) = P(a, b) / P(b) is the one used in the lecture.
questions.explanation: That quotient is the definition used to get conditionals from the joint.

questions.stem: In the weather table, P(hot, sun) = 0.4 and P(hot, rain) = 0.1, so P(hot) = 0.4.
questions.explanation: P(hot) = 0.4 + 0.1 = 0.5. P(sun | hot) is the 0.8 figure.

questions.stem: A missing arc in a Bayes net asserts a conditional independence.
questions.explanation: Missing arcs are the conditional independences encoded by the graph.

questions.stem: In the alarm network, P(burglary) = 0.01.
A Boolean child with two Boolean parents has 4 free CPT parameters.
questions.explanation: Free parameters are (d-1) times the product of the parent domain sizes: 1 * 2 * 2 = 4.

questions.stem: The Bayes-net chain rule multiplies P(Xi given every earlier variable), with no reduction to the parents.
questions.explanation: The net factorises as the product of P(Xi | Parents(Xi)).

questions.stem: In the alarm network, P(John calls | alarm) = 0.90 and P(John calls | no alarm) = 0.05.
questions.explanation: Those are the John CPT rows.

questions.stem: Exact inference by enumerating the hidden variables is linear in the number of variables for every network.
questions.explanation: The naive sum has exponentially many terms. A tree of local causes is the case that stays small.

questions.stem: An MDP specifies states, actions, a transition probability T(s, a, s'), and a reward on the transition.
questions.explanation: Those four, plus a start state and discounted additive utility, define the MDP.

questions.stem: The discount gamma must be 1, otherwise the infinite sum 1/(1-gamma) is not defined.
questions.explanation: gamma is in [0, 1). The sum 1/(1-gamma) is for a discount strictly below 1.

questions.stem: In reinforcement learning the agent does not know the transition model or the reward function and must try actions.
questions.explanation: Learning uses samples (s, a, s', r) because T and R are unknown.

questions.stem: Passive learning chooses which action to try next.
questions.explanation: Passive learning evaluates a fixed policy. The agent does not choose actions.

questions.stem: Temporal-difference learning moves V(s) toward the one-step sample r + gamma * V(s') after each transition.
questions.explanation: The update is a running average toward that one-step target.

questions.stem: The Q table has one entry per state, the same size as the V table.
questions.explanation: Q has one entry per state-action pair, so the table is larger than V.

questions.stem: The max over the next state's actions is what makes the Q-learning update off-policy.
questions.explanation: The max looks one optimal step ahead, so the data-collection policy need not be optimal.

questions.stem: Epsilon-greedy with a high fixed epsilon stops taking random actions once the values have settled.
questions.explanation: A high fixed epsilon keeps acting at random after the values are known. Lower it over time.

questions.stem: Regret is the gap between the rewards actually collected and the rewards of always acting optimally.
questions.explanation: Regret includes the cost of early mistakes.

questions.stem: Direct evaluation shares successor values between states, which is why it learns quickly.
questions.explanation: Direct evaluation learns each state's returns separately and wastes the links between states.

questions.stem: Predicting loan default from records with known outcomes is supervised classification.
questions.explanation: Known default outcomes make this supervised classification.

questions.stem: Grouping viewers from behaviour, with no labels, is supervised regression.
questions.explanation: No labels means unsupervised clustering.

questions.stem: Allocating CPU and memory, with a score based on response time and energy, is reinforcement learning.
questions.explanation: The score is a reward for a sequence of allocation actions.

questions.stem: Predicting energy in kWh is a classification task because the inputs are numeric.
questions.explanation: kWh is continuous, so the energy task is supervised regression.

questions.stem: The fitted energy line in the solution is energy = 302.26 - 6.19 * temperature.
questions.explanation: That is the solution line. The negative slope is a heating-dominated building.

questions.stem: At 15 degrees C that line predicts about 302 kWh.
R^2 = 0.948 means 94.8% of the variation in the training data is explained. It does not score new days.
questions.explanation: R^2 here is an in-sample figure. It does not measure a future day.

questions.stem: A negative temperature coefficient means warmer days use more energy.
questions.explanation: The negative coefficient means warmer days use less energy.

questions.stem: A few clinician-labelled records plus many unlabelled records is a semi-supervised setting.
questions.explanation: A small labelled set plus a large unlabelled set is semi-supervised learning.

questions.stem: On this linear model, equal steps in temperature produce unequal steps in predicted energy.
questions.explanation: A linear model changes the prediction by the same amount for each equal temperature step.

questions.stem: Logistic regression outputs a probability in (0, 1). A perceptron outputs a hard class.
questions.explanation: Those are the lab's output types for the two classifiers.

questions.stem: XOR is linearly separable, so one perceptron can represent it.
questions.explanation: XOR is the standard non-separable case. One perceptron cannot represent it.

questions.stem: The perceptron convergence theorem applies when the training set is linearly separable.
questions.explanation: Linear separability is the condition for a finite number of updates.

questions.stem: That theorem also promises that the separator it finds is the unique optimal one.
questions.explanation: The separator need not be unique, and one pass need not be enough.

questions.stem: In the lab update rule, a correct prediction leaves the weights unchanged.
questions.explanation: The update is proportional to (y - prediction), which is 0 when the prediction is correct.

questions.stem: The learning trace starts from weights [1, 1, 1].
questions.explanation: The trace starts at [0, 0, -1].

questions.stem: After the misclassified point [3, 2, 1] with learning rate 0.5, the weights are [1.5, 1, -0.5].
questions.explanation: The update is 0.5 * (1 - 0) * [3, 2, 1] added to [0, 0, -1].

questions.stem: One pass over the five lab points is enough to finish learning.
questions.explanation: The fixed weights [0.5, -0.5, -1] still miss points, and further epochs are required.

questions.stem: Linear regression can output any real number and is trained with squared error.
questions.explanation: That row of the lab comparison is linear regression.

questions.stem: Logistic regression uses a non-linear decision boundary.
questions.explanation: Logistic regression's boundary is linear. The sigmoid changes the output into a probability.

questions.stem: With input (0.5, -0.5), the first hidden pre-activation is 0.75 and ReLU leaves it at 0.75.
The second hidden pre-activation is -2, so ReLU returns -2.
questions.explanation: ReLU(-2) = 0. The unit is off on this example.

questions.stem: The linear network output on this step is 1.625.
questions.explanation: z = 1.5*0.75 + (-1)*0 + 0.5 = 1.625, and the output is linear.

questions.stem: The half squared loss on this step is about 1.625.
A positive partial derivative means the gradient step subtracts from that weight.
questions.explanation: The worked step subtracts eta times a positive gradient.

questions.stem: The derivative of ReLU is 1 for every negative input.
questions.explanation: ReLU's derivative is 0 for z <= 0.

questions.stem: Hidden unit 2 gets a zero gradient on this example, so its weights do not change.
questions.explanation: A zero ReLU blocks both the activation and the gradient on this step.

questions.stem: Leaky ReLU also has derivative 0 on negative inputs.
questions.explanation: Leaky ReLU and ELU keep a small gradient for negative inputs.

questions.stem: The target on this worked example is 1.
questions.explanation: The worked target is y = 1.

questions.stem: The output pre-activation 1.5 * 0.75 + (-1) * 0 + 0.5 equals 0.75.
questions.explanation: That expression equals 1.625, which is the network output.

questions.stem: For the 2-4-1 XOR net, W1 has shape (2, 4) and W2 has shape (4, 1).
questions.explanation: X is (4, 2), so W1 must be (2, 4). W2 maps 4 hidden units to 1 output.

questions.stem: This lab implements dropout and weight decay from the model-selection lecture.
questions.explanation: The lab trains the XOR network from Lecture 7. Dropout and weight decay are Lecture 8 theory.

questions.stem: If every weight starts at the same value, hidden units receive the same gradient. That is the symmetry problem.
questions.explanation: Equal initial weights make the hidden units learn the same feature.

questions.stem: sigmoid(0) equals 0.
questions.explanation: sigmoid(0) = 0.5.

questions.stem: The derivative of the sigmoid is at most 0.25.
questions.explanation: s(1-s) reaches 0.25 at s = 0.5 and is smaller elsewhere.

questions.stem: The 2-4-1 XOR net has 23,860 parameters.
questions.explanation: The XOR net has 2*4 + 4 + 4*1 + 1 = 17 parameters. 23,860 is the larger 784-30-10 example.

questions.stem: The lab loss is the mean of 0.5 * (output - target)^2, so the output gradient simplifies to (output - target).
questions.explanation: The 1/2 cancels the 2 from differentiating the square, leaving (A2 - y).

questions.stem: Thresholding the learned XOR outputs at 0.5 fails to recover the four target labels.
questions.explanation: The learned outputs are about 0.03, 0.97, 0.97, 0.03, so a 0.5 threshold recovers 0, 1, 1, 0.

questions.stem: Biases may start at 0, because each unit has its own bias.
questions.explanation: The symmetry warning is about equal weights. Distinct biases can start at 0.

questions.stem: A NaN loss in this lab usually means the learning rate is too small.
questions.explanation: NaN usually means overflow from a huge learning rate or a missing factor in the loss.

questions.stem: The five-house set has 3 Yes and 2 No labels, so its entropy is about 0.971 bits.
Furniture has the highest information gain at the root.
questions.explanation: Furniture gains 0.020 bits. Number of rooms gains 0.420.

questions.stem: The root test is number of rooms, with information gain about 0.420 bits.
questions.explanation: Rooms beats New kitchen (0.171) and Furniture (0.020).

questions.stem: The rooms = 4 branch is mixed, so the tree next tests Furniture there.
questions.explanation: Houses 3 and 5 are both Yes, so rooms = 4 is a Yes leaf.

questions.stem: On the rooms = 3 subset, New kitchen has higher information gain than Furniture.
questions.explanation: On that subset the gains are 0.918 for New kitchen and 0.251 for Furniture.

questions.stem: A new house with 4 rooms and no new kitchen is predicted No.
questions.explanation: Four rooms is Yes regardless of the other features.

questions.stem: Furniture does not appear in the learned tree.
questions.explanation: The second split is New kitchen, and Furniture is unused.

questions.stem: The learned tree misclassifies house 5.
questions.explanation: House 5 has 4 rooms and falls in the Yes leaf. All five training rows are classified.

questions.stem: A prediction is a walk from the root to a leaf.
questions.explanation: Each internal node is one test, and the leaf is the prediction.

questions.stem: At the root, New kitchen has higher information gain than number of rooms.
questions.explanation: At the root, rooms (0.420) beats New kitchen (0.171).

questions.stem: Assignment 1's maze task requires IDS, A*, and IDA*.
questions.explanation: The required maze algorithms are IDS, A*, and IDA*.

questions.stem: Legal maze moves include diagonal steps.
questions.explanation: Moves are one step to an adjacent open cell. Diagonals and walls are forbidden.

questions.stem: When every move has the same cost, path cost equals the number of moves.
questions.explanation: Unit step costs make cost equal to path length.

questions.stem: IDA* bounds each iteration by depth alone, exactly as IDS does.
questions.explanation: IDA* raises an f = g + h bound. IDS raises a depth bound.

questions.stem: An admissible maze heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost.
questions.explanation: Admissible means a lower bound on the remaining cost.

questions.stem: Crossword variables are the individual letter cells, with no word slots.
questions.explanation: Variables are word slots, the maximal across and down sequences.

questions.stem: MRV selects the variable with the fewest remaining legal values.
questions.explanation: Fewest remaining values is the fail-first variable order.

questions.stem: LCV tries first the value that rules out the most options in neighbouring variables.
questions.explanation: LCV tries the value that eliminates the fewest options in neighbouring domains.

questions.stem: AC-3 keeps revising queued arcs until no domain shrinks further, or some domain becomes empty.
questions.explanation: AC-3 processes the arc queue until a fixed point or an empty domain.

questions.stem: If the maze destination is fully blocked, a correct solver should still return a path through walls.
questions.explanation: An unreachable destination should be reported as no solution, and the search should stop.

questions.stem: A 28 by 28 grayscale image gives 784 input features.
questions.explanation: 28 * 28 = 784 features.

questions.stem: The submitted training-history plot starts its x-axis at epoch 0.
questions.explanation: The submitted plot uses epoch numbers starting at 1. The stored best_epoch index is zero-based.

questions.stem: The required softmax regression model is 784-10.
questions.explanation: Softmax regression here is a 784-10 model.

questions.stem: Learning rate 1.0 was totally unstable and produced NaN loss.
questions.explanation: Rate 1.0 stayed finite but oscillated. Rates 10 and 100 produced NaN loss.

questions.stem: The assignment forbids sklearn, PyTorch, and TensorFlow for the learning algorithms.
questions.explanation: Those libraries are disallowed for the algorithms.

questions.stem: The console figures in the report are screenshots captured from a terminal window.
questions.explanation: plot_results.py draws selected log lines with Matplotlib.

questions.stem: Pixel values are scaled by dividing by 255.
questions.explanation: Inputs are scaled by dividing pixel values by 255.

questions.stem: A residual addition works when the two hidden widths differ, with no extra projection.
questions.explanation: A residual add needs matching widths, or the constructor raises ValueError.

questions.stem: Reusing the default full-data two-layer run leaves 19 distinct experiment runs.
questions.explanation: 12 baseline runs, plus 4 extra learning rates, plus 3 extra batch sizes.

questions.stem: The submitted code zip must include results/summary.csv.
questions.explanation: The zip contains the four Python files. The CSV is created by run_experiments.py.

questions.stem: A hypothesis is consistent when it matches every training pair. Among consistent hypotheses, Ockham's razor prefers the one with fewer assumptions. A hypothesis can be consistent and still be a poor predictor on new data.
questions.explanation: Consistency is a training-set property. Ockham then prefers the simpler consistent hypothesis. A curve through every noisy point can still fail on the next point.

questions.stem: Every consistent heuristic is admissible. Consistency is the further requirement used to guarantee that A* graph search is optimal.
questions.explanation: The triangle inequality implies the heuristic never overestimates, so consistency is the stronger condition. Graph search needs that stronger condition.

questions.stem: Iterative deepening uses O(bd) memory. When every step cost is equal, it is optimal.
questions.explanation: Iterative deepening stores one depth-first path, O(bd), and with equal step costs the first goal it reaches is a shallowest, hence cheapest, goal.

questions.stem: A CSP solution is an assignment that gives every variable a value and breaks no constraint. A partial assignment that breaks nothing is not yet a solution.
questions.explanation: The course definition requires both words: complete, and consistent. A legal partial assignment is unfinished.

questions.stem: In CSP backtracking, minimum remaining values and the degree heuristic choose the next variable. Least constraining value chooses the next value for the variable already chosen.
questions.explanation: Minimum remaining values, with degree as the tie break, selects the variable. Least constraining value orders the values of that variable.

questions.stem: If the training set is linearly separable, the perceptron reaches some separating weights after a finite number of updates. That theorem does not promise that one pass is enough, and it does not promise a unique separator.
questions.explanation: Separability gives finite convergence to some separator. It does not give one-epoch convergence or a unique line.

questions.stem: For a sigmoid output s, the local derivative factor s(1 - s) is at most 0.25. Stacking several sigmoid layers can therefore make the gradient that reaches the earliest layer very small.
questions.explanation: s(1 - s) peaks at 0.25 when s = 0.5, and is near 0 when s is near 0 or 1. Each sigmoid layer can multiply the backward signal by at most 1/4.

questions.stem: In a Bayes net, once a variable's parents are known, that variable is conditionally independent of its non-descendants.
questions.explanation: That is the local independence claim that lets the joint equal the product of P(variable | its parents).

questions.stem: If ID3 has no attributes left and the remaining examples still contain both class labels, it returns the majority class of those remaining examples.
questions.explanation: Mixed labels with no attribute left are labelled by the majority of the rows still at that node. An empty set of rows would instead use the parent's majority.

questions.stem: The Q-learning target is r + gamma * max over a' of Q(s', a'). It uses the best next action in the table, not whichever action the behaviour policy takes in s'.
questions.explanation: The max is what makes the update off-policy. The action actually taken in s' is not the action inside the target.

questions.stem: Breadth-first search is optimal for every set of positive step costs, because it expands the tree one layer at a time.
questions.explanation: Layer order minimises the number of steps. If step costs differ, fewer steps can cost more, so breadth-first search is not optimal.

questions.stem: An admissible heuristic is enough to guarantee that A* graph search returns an optimal path.
questions.explanation: Admissibility is the tree-search condition. Graph search can discard a repeated state along a path whose f looked good only because h was inconsistent.

questions.stem: Hill climbing that is allowed to move sideways, with no cap on how many sideways moves it may take, is guaranteed to leave every plateau.
questions.explanation: A shoulder can have an uphill exit, but a flat plateau may not. With no cap, sideways moves can also loop. The course caps sideways moves, for example at 100.

questions.stem: The directed arc X -> Y is consistent when every remaining value of Y has at least one remaining value of X that satisfies the constraint.
questions.explanation: The arc X -> Y constrains the tail. Every remaining value of X must have a support in Y. The statement runs the check in the other direction.

questions.stem: Temporal-difference policy evaluation needs a known transition model T. Without T it cannot form the target r + gamma * V(s').
questions.explanation: The sampled next state stands in for the unknown transition. Temporal-difference policy evaluation does not need T. It also cannot, by itself, choose between actions.

questions.stem: Full gradient descent steps on a mini-batch of 32 to 512 rows. Stochastic gradient descent waits until the gradient has been computed on every training row, then steps once.
questions.explanation: The two methods are swapped. Full gradient descent uses every training row for one step. A mini-batch of 32 to 512 is stochastic gradient descent, as the slides use that term.

questions.stem: Early stopping keeps the weights from the epoch with the lowest training loss.
questions.explanation: The checkpoint is the best validation epoch. Training loss can keep falling after that point, which is the overfitting signal.

questions.stem: A residual connection is a regulariser. Its job is to shrink the gap between training error and test error.
questions.explanation: A residual connection is an optimisation device: the block learns a change added to its input, and the skip path helps the gradient. It is not, by itself, a regulariser.

questions.stem: Raw information gain is a safe score for an attribute such as a unique student identifier. Pure children are exactly what ID3 should reward, so that attribute should be the root.
questions.explanation: A unique identifier splits the rows into pure singletons, so raw gain looks perfect and the tree memorises identities. Gain ratio penalises attributes with many values.

questions.stem: With discount gamma = 1, an infinite sequence of rewards equal to +1 has total utility 1.
questions.explanation: With gamma = 1 the sum 1 + 1 + 1 + ... does not converge. The closed form 1 / (1 - gamma) needs gamma < 1.
